body:
## What

`enter_cbor_array` and `enter_msgpack_array` now enter the scalar run (#5975, #5980) only for arrays of **two or more** elements. Before, they entered it for every non-empty array: `len == 0` is now `len <= 1`.

```cpp
return enter_array(len) && (len <= 1 || parse_cbor_scalar_run(std::integral_constant<bool, bulk_scan> {}));
```

It is the same comparison, with no extra instruction and no extra branch, so arrays of two or more elements run exactly the same code as before.

## Why: the nested-array regression came back

The scalar run is `JSON_HEDLEY_NEVER_INLINE`, so that `parse_cbor_value` / `parse_msgpack_value` stay small enough to inline. Entering it is a real call: the prologue saves the callee-saved registers the loop needs, the loop tests the remaining count and length, the switch finds a head it does not handle, and the epilogue restores the registers. For an array whose first element is an object, an array or a string, all of that reads nothing.

On most documents this costs nothing measurable, because it happens once per array, not once per element. It matters when the arrays themselves are the work, i.e. many small arrays whose element is a container. The benchmark `FromBinaryShape/nested` is the extreme case: 1,000 arrays nested in each other, each with exactly one element.

This was already found and fixed once, inside #5975:

1. *address review of the scalar-run reader* removed the first pre-check, `cbor_scalar_follows()`.
2. *enter the scalar run only when a scalar follows* added it back, because "on nested data (arrays of objects) that call made reading slower than before the run reader". The MessagePack PR #5980 got the same pre-check.
3. *drop the scalar pre-check before the run* removed it again in both PRs. The measurements in that commit cover canada and the nativejson files, not the nested shape, so the regression from step 2 returned without anyone seeing it.

The suite run for the 3.13.0 blog post on 11-02 caught it. `FromBinaryShape/nested` got 4.6 % (CBOR) and 2.5 % (MessagePack) slower than a build that still had the pre-check. Compared with no scalar run at all, nested arrays cost:

| | CBOR | MessagePack |
|---|---|---|
| GCC 13, instructions (callgrind) | +3.7 % | +4.3 % |
| Apple clang, time (blog A/B) | +6 to +8 % | +6 to +8 % |

## Why `len <= 1` and not the pre-check again

The pre-check cost exactly what the third commit said: one inline test of the remaining length and the head byte on every array that does enter the run. canada's `[x, y]` pairs and the `[1, 2]` arrays of `FromBinaryShape/containers` pay it 100,000 times.

The element count is already in a register, and the comparison against 0 is already there. Testing `<= 1` instead of `== 0` is free. It catches the shape that actually hurts, because each level of a chain of nested arrays holds one element. The same holds for the single ring of a GeoJSON `Polygon` (`[[[x, y], ...]]`) and for one-element arrays of objects.

What it gives up is arrays of **one scalar**, such as `[7]`. The run reads a lone scalar faster than the general path does, so those get slower (see below). They are rare in real documents:

| Arrays in the document | citm_catalog | twitter | canada |
|---|---|---|---|
| all arrays | 10,451 | 1,050 | 56,045 |
| one element, a container (helped) | 124 | 139 | 1 |
| one element, a scalar (slower) | **1** | **0** | **0** |
| ≥ 2 elements, first a container (still one call) | 1,270 | 9 | 481 |

## Measurements

All with ab-harness: develop (b2674a4a2f) and this branch compiled into one binary, renamed namespaces, both link orders.

- **GCC 13 on x86-64:** callgrind instruction counts. These are exact, with no noise.
- **Mac (M1 Max, Apple clang 21):** instructions retired, minimum of 3 runs, plus timings over 4 layouts × 25 alternating pairs.

Each workload is one `from_cbor` / `from_msgpack` of a value, B/A = this PR / develop:

- `nested`: 1,000 arrays nested in each other.
- `singles`: 100,000 arrays `[i]`.
- `containers`: 100,000 arrays `[1, 2]`.
- `scalars`: one array of 1,000,000 integers.
- `objects`: one array of 20,000 objects of two members.
- `canada`, `twitter`, `citm_catalog`: the nativejson-benchmark files.

| Workload | GCC 13 instr CBOR | GCC 13 instr MsgPack | Mac instr CBOR | Mac instr MsgPack | Mac time CBOR | Mac time MsgPack |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| nested | **0.973** | **0.971** | **0.944** | **0.952** | **0.950** | **0.961** |
| singles | *1.037* | *1.021* | *1.049* | *1.033* | *1.043* | *1.035* |
| containers | 0.998 | 0.999 | 0.996 | 1.005 | | |
| scalars | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | 1.000 | | |
| objects | 0.999 | 1.000 | 1.002 | 1.000 | | |
| canada | 0.999 | 0.999 | 1.000 | 1.002 | 1.000 | |
| twitter | 0.999 | 1.000 | 1.007 | 1.001 | | |
| citm_catalog | 0.999 | 1.000 | 0.999 | 1.000 | 1.000 | |

Mac instruction counts of allocation-heavy cases drift by up to ±1 % between runs (twitter, CBOR containers here). The exact GCC counts are the reference.

On GCC, this PR recovers 2.7 to 2.9 points of the 3.7 to 4.3 % that the run costs nested arrays. I did not look into where the last point comes from. A build without the run at all is not an option: it makes canada 6 to 10 % and flat scalar arrays 57 to 80 % more expensive.

The suite's own rows (`json_benchmarks`, Apple clang with LTO) agree in direction. These are two separate binaries built from this branch's `benchmarks.cpp` with develop's and this PR's header, run alternately: median of 3 runs × 5 repetitions each. The load was 3 to 5 during the runs and the run-to-run spread was up to 3.5 %, so read only the two shapes this PR targets:

| Row | develop | this PR | PR/develop |
|---|---|---|---|
| FromBinaryShape/nested / cbor | 38.0 µs | 35.3 µs | **0.929** |
| FromBinaryShape/nested / msgpack | 37.1 µs | 35.2 µs | **0.946** |
| FromBinaryShape/singles / cbor | 3.68 ms | 3.96 ms | *1.074* |
| FromBinaryShape/singles / msgpack | 3.64 ms | 3.92 ms | *1.075* |
| FromBinaryShape/containers / cbor | 3.93 ms | 3.97 ms | 1.010 |
| FromBinaryShape/containers / msgpack | 3.88 ms | 3.89 ms | 1.003 |
| FromBinaryShape/scalars / cbor | 5.69 ms | 5.70 ms | 1.002 |
| FromBinaryShape/scalars / msgpack | 5.62 ms | 5.58 ms | 0.993 |
| FromBinaryFile/cbor / canada | 4.57 ms | 4.54 ms | 0.995 |
| FromBinaryFile/cbor / twitter | 1.59 ms | 1.57 ms | 0.989 |

The suite shows `singles` 7.5 % slower, more than the harness's 3.5 to 4.3 %. The harness pairs its samples and alternates both link orders, so its number is the more reliable one.

### Variants measured and not taken

Same workloads, GCC 13 callgrind instructions, B/A against develop (CBOR / MessagePack). Worst rows only:

| Variant | nested | cost elsewhere |
|---|---|---|
| **this PR: `len <= 1`** | **0.973 / 0.971** | singles 1.037 / 1.021, everything else ±0.15 % |
| inline pre-check on every array (the one removed in #5975) | 0.979 / 0.980 | canada 1.006 / 1.016, containers 1.007 / 1.016 |
| pre-check only for one-element arrays | 0.979 / 0.981 | singles 1.009 / 1.019, canada and containers up to 1.009 |
| early exit at the top of the run | 0.992 / 0.991 | scalars 1.022 / 1.023, canada 1.011 / 1.014 |
| early exit and a do-while loop | 0.992 / 0.987 | scalars 1.011 / 1.023 |

The two early-exit variants looked good on the Mac (nested −3.6 to −4.0 %), but on GCC they add one to two instructions per element to the loop itself.

## What does not change

- Values, SAX events, errors and error positions are the same: a one-element array is read by `parse_cbor_value` / `parse_msgpack_value`, which is what the run falls back to anyway.
- Non-contiguous input never entered the run and is unaffected.
- Arrays of two or more elements whose first element is a container still pay one call per array, as before. citm has 1,270 of them, and none of the measured rows moves.

## Keeping it from coming back

- The doc comment of `enter_cbor_array` says why one-element arrays stay out. It also names the two benchmarks that show the trade-off.
- New benchmark rows `FromBinaryShape/singles / cbor` and `/ msgpack` (100,000 arrays `[i]`). They make the other side of the trade-off visible in the suite, next to `FromBinaryShape/nested`.

## Tests

New test cases "CBOR arrays of one element from contiguous and non-contiguous input" and the MessagePack counterpart. They read a document with one-element arrays:

- a chain `[[[[1.5]]]]`,
- `[7]`,
- `[{"x": 2.5}]`,
- `["s"]`,
- `[[1, 2]]`,
- `[null]`.

Each array is followed by enough bytes that the run could have been entered. The tests check the value, then compare contiguous (`std::vector`) against byte-wise (`std::list`) input for every truncation of the document: the `from_cbor` / `from_msgpack` result or exception message, and the full SAX event log.

`unit-cbor` and `unit-msgpack` pass: 250,838 and 245,979 assertions.

## Breaking changes

None. Values, errors, error positions and SAX events are unchanged, and the public API is untouched.

title: CBOR/MessagePack readers: leave one-element arrays to the general path
